topic: The Pi Machine: How Colliding Blocks Calculate Geometry
target_audience: High school physics students and undergraduate math enthusiasts

outline.topic: The Pi Machine: How Colliding Blocks Calculate Geometry
outline.target_audience: High school physics students and undergraduate math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Setup: An Unlikely Experiment
sections.content: Introduce a frictionless environment with a wall, a small block (mass m), and a much larger block (mass M). The large block slides toward the small block, which is sitting between the wall and the large block. We will count every 'clack': collisions between blocks and collisions with the wall.
sections.example: Imagine a tiny hamster in a 1kg box and a massive elephant on a 100kg skateboard gliding toward it.

sections.title: The Pattern: Digits of Pi Reveal Themselves
sections.content: Observe the results as we increase the mass ratio in powers of 100 (1:100^n). Show that for M=1, collisions = 3. For M=100, collisions = 31. For M=10,000, collisions = 314. The total count matches the digits of π.
sections.example: A digital counter above the blocks ticks up: 3, 31, 314, 3141... as the 'elephant' block gets exponentially heavier.

sections.title: Prerequisites: Energy and Momentum
sections.content: Explain the two laws governing each collision: Conservation of Momentum (mv + MV = constant) and Conservation of Kinetic Energy (1/2mv² + 1/2MV² = constant). Introduce the velocity state space where the x-axis is 'v' (small block) and the y-axis is 'V' (large block).
sections.example: Visualizing the Energy equation as a stretched ellipse on a coordinate plane, where every point represents the speeds of both blocks.

sections.title: The Circle Transformation
sections.content: To simplify the math, we rescale the coordinates (multiplying the velocity by the square root of the mass). This transformation turns the energy ellipse into a perfect circle. Now, every collision corresponds to a point moving along the perimeter of this circle.
sections.example: An animation showing the 'squashed' ellipse being pulled vertically until it becomes a perfect geometric circle, making the physics symmetric.

sections.title: The Geometry of 'Clacks'
sections.content: Explain that each collision is a jump along the circle. The 'distance' of each jump is determined by the mass ratio. Because the total path of the blocks moving towards and then away from the wall covers exactly half the circle (an angle of π), the number of jumps relates directly to the ratio of the arc length.
sections.example: A laser beam bouncing inside a circular mirror, where each 'bounce' represents a collision, slowly tracing out the arc of π.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why Pi?
sections.content: Summarize that the number of collisions is the integer part of π divided by the angle of the 'jump'. As the large mass increases, the angle becomes smaller, allowing more 'jumps' to fit into the π arc, effectively extracting the decimal digits of π.
sections.example: The 'Pi-Block' device finishes its 314th clack, and the camera zooms out to show the blocks have traced a perfect semi-circle on the floor map.

storyboard.title: The Setup: An Unlikely Experiment
lecture_lines: Two blocks and a wall on a frictionless surface.
A large block M slides toward a small block m.
We count every collision between blocks and the wall.
animations: Create a white vertical line for the wall (#FFFFFF) and a horizontal line for the floor (#FFFFFF).
Draw a small blue square (#0000FF) labeled 'm' near the wall.
Draw a large red square (#FF0000) labeled 'M' sliding from right to left toward 'm'.

storyboard.title: The Pattern: Digits of Pi Reveal Themselves
lecture_lines: If M and m are equal, we count 3 clacks.
Increasing M by powers of 100 reveals digits.
Surprisingly, these counts perfectly match the digits of pi.
animations: Show two equal blocks colliding; a counter (#FFFF00) increments to 3.
Reset; change M to 100; the counter quickly ticks to 31.
Reset; change M to 10,000; the counter ticks rapidly to 314.
The counter value 314 turns into the symbol π (#FFD700).
Flash the digits 3.14159... in the center of the screen (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Prerequisites: Energy and Momentum
lecture_lines: Momentum and kinetic energy are conserved in every collision.
We can plot velocities v and V as a point.
Energy conservation defines a state-space trajectory.
This path forms a squashed ellipse on the graph.
Every collision shifts our position along this curve.
animations: Display the formula 'mv + MV = p' in green (#00FF00) at the top.
Display '1/2mv² + 1/2MV² = E' in yellow (#FFFF00) below the first.
Create a coordinate plane with axes 'v' and 'V' in white (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Circle Transformation
lecture_lines: We rescale the coordinates using the mass ratio.
This transformation stretches the ellipse into a perfect circle.
Now, every collision is just a jump along the circle.
The physics becomes symmetric and easier to visualize.
All possible states now lie on a constant radius.
animations: Draw a thin, horizontal ellipse (#FF00FF) on the (v, V) plane.
Highlight the V-axis label and show it multiplying by sqrt(M/m) (#FFFFFF).
Animate the ellipse morphing into a perfect circle (#00FFFF).
Mark a point on the circle that 'jumps' to a new spot (#FFFF00).
Draw a line from the origin to the new point to show the angle (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Geometry of 'Clacks'
lecture_lines: Each collision rotates the state by a specific angle.
This angle depends on the ratio of the masses.
The total process sweeps through exactly pi radians.
Counting collisions is like fitting steps into an arc.
Thus, the total count reveals the digits of pi.
animations: Show a point on the circle (#00FFFF) jumping repeatedly along the perimeter.
Draw an arc (#FF8C00) between two successive points to show the step.
Fade in dashed lines representing reflections during collisions (#888888).
Highlight the semicircular arc with the label π in gold (#FFD700).
Draw many small jumps filling the semi-circle to represent large M (#00FFFF).

storyboard.title: Conclusion: Why Pi?
lecture_lines: Pi emerges from the geometry of energy and momentum.
Heavy masses create smaller steps, revealing more digits.
A beautiful link between simple collisions and fundamental constants.
animations: Display 'Collisions = floor(π / θ)' in large white text (#FFFFFF).
Show the block counter (#FFFF00) and the circle side-by-side to sync them.
Final fade out with the symbol π glowing in gold (#FFD700).
